title: CoDeTT: A Context-Aware Decision Benchmark for Turn-Taking Evaluation
summary: Turn-taking modeling is fundamental to spoken dialogue systems, yet its evaluation remains fragmented and often limited to binary boundary detection under narrow interaction settings. Such protocols hinder systematic comparison and obscure model weaknesses across conversational conditions. We present CoDeTT, a context-aware decision benchmark for turn-taking evaluation. CoDeTT formulates turn-taking as a structured decision problem and constructs a multi-scenario dataset with fine-grained decision categories and controlled context variations. Under a unified evaluation protocol, we assess representative existing models and observe substantial performance disparities across decision types and interaction scenarios. CoDeTT provides a standardized benchmark for systematic and context-aware evaluation of turn-taking systems. The benchmark dataset and evaluation toolkit are available at https://github.com/YingaoWang-casia/CoDeTT.github.io.

AI.tldr: CoDeTT is a context-aware benchmark for evaluating turn-taking models as structured decision problems across multiple scenarios with fine-grained categories and controlled context variations.
AI.motivation: Current turn-taking evaluation is fragmented, limited to binary boundary detection in narrow settings, hindering systematic comparison and obscuring model weaknesses across different conversational conditions.
AI.method: Formulates turn-taking as a structured decision problem, constructs a multi-scenario dataset with fine-grained decision categories and controlled context variations, and implements a unified evaluation protocol.
AI.result: Assessment of representative existing models reveals substantial performance disparities across decision types and interaction scenarios, demonstrating the benchmark's ability to identify model weaknesses.
AI.conclusion: CoDeTT provides a standardized benchmark for systematic and context-aware evaluation of turn-taking systems, with publicly available dataset and evaluation toolkit.

title: Dominant Transient Stability of the Co-located PLL-Based Grid-Following Renewable Plant and Synchronous Condenser Systems
summary: Deploying synchronous condensers (SynCons) near grid-following renewable energy sources (GFLRs) is an effective and increasingly adopted strategy for grid support. However, the potential transient instability risks in such configurations remain an open research question. This study investigates the mechanism of dominant synchronization instability source transition upon SynCon integration and proposes a straightforward approach to enhance system stability by leveraging their interactive characteristics. Firstly, a dual-timescale decoupling model is established, partitioning the system into a fast subsystem representing phase-locked loop (PLL) dynamics and a slow subsystem characterizing SynCon rotor dynamics. The study then examines the influence of SynCons on the transient stability of nearby PLLs and their own inherent stability. The study shows that SynCon's voltage-source characteristics and its time-scale separation from PLL dynamics can significantly enhance the PLL's stability boundary and mitigate non-coherent coupling effects among multiple GFLRs. However, the dominant instability source shifts from the fast-time-scale PLL to the slow-time-scale SynCon after SynCon integration. Crucially, this paper demonstrates that the damping effect of PLL control can also be transferred from the fast to the slow time scale, allowing well-tuned PLL damping to suppress SynCon rotor acceleration. Consequently, by utilizing SynCon's inherent support capability and a simple PLL damping loop, the transient stability of the co-located system can be significantly enhanced. These conclusions are validated using a converter controller-based Hardware-in-the-Loop (CHIL) platform.

AI.tldr: SynCon integration near GFLRs enhances PLL stability but shifts dominant instability source to SynCon rotor dynamics; PLL damping can suppress SynCon rotor acceleration, enabling significant transient stability improvement.
AI.motivation: While synchronous condenser deployment near grid-following renewable sources is effective for grid support, the transient instability risks in such configurations remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding how instability sources transition and how system stability can be enhanced through interactive characteristics.
AI.method: Established a dual-timescale decoupling model separating fast PLL dynamics and slow SynCon rotor dynamics; analyzed SynCon's influence on PLL transient stability and SynCon's inherent stability; investigated instability source transition and damping transfer mechanisms; validated using converter controller-based Hardware-in-the-Loop platform.
AI.result: SynCon's voltage-source characteristics and timescale separation enhance PLL stability boundary and mitigate non-coherent coupling among multiple GFLRs; dominant instability source shifts from fast PLL to slow SynCon after integration; PLL damping can be transferred to suppress SynCon rotor acceleration; combined SynCon support and PLL damping significantly enhance co-located system transient stability.
AI.conclusion: SynCon integration fundamentally changes system instability dynamics by shifting dominant instability source from PLL to SynCon rotor, but this can be leveraged by transferring PLL damping to suppress SynCon acceleration, enabling simple yet effective stability enhancement through coordinated control.

title: On Port-Hamiltonian Formulation of HystereticEnergy Storage Elements: The Backlash Case
summary: This paper presents a port-Hamiltonian formulation of hysteretic energy storage elements. First, we revisit the passivity property of backlash-driven storage elements by presenting a family of storage functions associated to the dissipativity property of such elements. We explicitly derive the corresponding available storage and required supply functions `a la Willems [1], and show the interlacing property of the aforementioned family of storage functions sandwiched between the available storage and required supply functions. Second, using the proposed family of storage functions, we present a port-Hamiltonian formulation of hysteretic inductors as prototypical storage elements in port-Hamiltonian systems. In particular, we show how a Hamiltonian function can be chosen from the family of storage functions and how the hysteretic elements can be expressed as port-Hamiltonian system with feedthrough term, where the feedthrough term represents energy dissipation. Correspondingly, we illustrate its applicability in describing an RLC circuit (in parallel and in series) containing a hysteretic inductor element.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a port-Hamiltonian framework for hysteretic energy storage elements, specifically focusing on hysteretic inductors, by deriving storage functions and demonstrating their application in RLC circuits.
AI.motivation: To establish a systematic port-Hamiltonian formulation for hysteretic energy storage elements, which are common in physical systems but lack a unified modeling framework within the port-Hamiltonian paradigm.
AI.method: 1. Revisit passivity of backlash-driven storage elements and derive a family of storage functions using Willems' dissipativity theory. 2. Explicitly compute available storage and required supply functions. 3. Show interlacing property of storage functions between available storage and required supply. 4. Use these storage functions to formulate hysteretic inductors as port-Hamiltonian systems with feedthrough terms representing energy dissipation. 5. Apply the formulation to RLC circuits (parallel and series) containing hysteretic inductors.
AI.result: Successfully derived a family of storage functions for hysteretic elements, established their relationship through interlacing property, and developed a port-Hamiltonian formulation for hysteretic inductors that includes feedthrough terms to account for energy dissipation. Demonstrated applicability through RLC circuit examples.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous port-Hamiltonian framework for modeling hysteretic energy storage elements, enabling systematic analysis and control design for systems containing such nonlinear elements while preserving the energy-based structure of port-Hamiltonian systems.

title: Feature Selection for Fault Prediction in Distribution Systems
summary: While conventional power system protection isolates faulty components only after a fault has occurred, fault prediction approaches try to detect faults before they can cause significant damage. Although initial studies have demonstrated successful proofs of concept, development is hindered by scarce field data and ineffective feature selection. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a surrogate task that uses simulation data for feature selection. This task exhibits a strong correlation (r = 0.92) with real-world fault prediction performance. We generate a large dataset containing 20000 simulations with 34 event classes and diverse grid configurations. From 1556 candidate features, we identify 374 optimal features. A case study on three substations demonstrates the effectiveness of the selected features, achieving an F1-score of 0.80 and outperforming baseline approaches that use frequency-domain and wavelet-based features.

AI.tldr: Proposes a surrogate task using simulation data for feature selection in power system fault prediction, achieving strong correlation with real-world performance and identifying optimal features that outperform baseline approaches.
AI.motivation: Conventional power system protection only isolates faults after they occur, while fault prediction aims to detect faults before damage. Development is hindered by scarce field data and ineffective feature selection.
AI.method: Proposes a surrogate task using simulation data for feature selection. Generates large dataset with 20,000 simulations, 34 event classes, and diverse grid configurations. Identifies 374 optimal features from 1,556 candidates.
AI.result: Surrogate task shows strong correlation (r = 0.92) with real-world fault prediction performance. Case study on three substations achieves F1-score of 0.80, outperforming baseline approaches using frequency-domain and wavelet-based features.
AI.conclusion: The proposed simulation-based surrogate task effectively addresses data scarcity and feature selection challenges in power system fault prediction, demonstrating practical utility through improved performance over conventional methods.

title: Entire Period Transient Stability of Synchronous Generators Considering LVRT Switching of Nearby Renewable Energy Sources
summary: In scenarios where synchronous generators (SGs) and grid-following renewable energy sources (GFLR) are co-located, existing research, which mainly focuses on the first-swing stability of SGs, often overlooks ongoing dynamic interactions between GFLRs and SGs throughout the entire rotor swing period. To address this gap, this study first reveals that the angle oscillations of SG can cause periodic grid voltage fluctuations, potentially triggering low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) control switching of GFLR repeatedly. Then, the periodic energy changes of SGs under "circular" and "rectangular" LVRT limits are analyzed. The results indicate that circular limits are detrimental to SG's first-swing stability, while rectangular limits and their slow recovery strategies can lead to SG's multi-swing instability. Conservative stability criteria are also proposed for these phenomena. Furthermore, an additional controller based on feedback linearization is introduced to enhance the entire period transient stability of SG by adjusting the post-fault GFLR output current. Finally, the efficacy of the analysis is validated through electromagnetic transient simulations and controller hardware-in-the-loop (CHIL) tests.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes dynamic interactions between synchronous generators (SGs) and grid-following renewable energy sources (GFLR) during rotor swing periods, revealing how SG angle oscillations trigger GFLR LVRT control switching, analyzes energy changes under different LVRT limits, proposes stability criteria, and introduces a feedback linearization controller to enhance SG transient stability.
AI.motivation: Existing research focuses on SG first-swing stability but overlooks ongoing dynamic interactions between GFLRs and SGs throughout the entire rotor swing period, particularly how SG angle oscillations can trigger repeated LVRT control switching of GFLRs.
AI.method: 1) Analysis of how SG angle oscillations cause periodic grid voltage fluctuations triggering GFLR LVRT control; 2) Energy analysis of SGs under "circular" and "rectangular" LVRT limits; 3) Development of conservative stability criteria; 4) Design of feedback linearization controller to adjust post-fault GFLR output current; 5) Validation through electromagnetic transient simulations and controller hardware-in-the-loop tests.
AI.result: Circular LVRT limits are detrimental to SG's first-swing stability, while rectangular limits and their slow recovery strategies can lead to SG's multi-swing instability. The proposed feedback linearization controller effectively enhances SG's entire period transient stability.
AI.conclusion: The study provides comprehensive analysis of SG-GFLR dynamic interactions during rotor swings, reveals stability issues with different LVRT limit types, proposes stability criteria, and demonstrates that a feedback linearization controller can effectively improve SG transient stability throughout the entire swing period.

title: DRL-Based Spectrum Sharing for RIS-Aided Local High-Quality Wireless Networks
summary: This paper investigates a smart spectrum-sharing framework for reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided local high-quality wireless networks (LHQWNs) within a mobile network operator (MNO) ecosystem. Although RISs are often considered potentially harmful due to interference, this work shows that properly controlled RISs can enhance the quality of service (QoS). The proposed system enables temporary spectrum access for multiple vertical service providers (VSPs) by dynamically allocating radio resources according to traffic demand. The spectrum is divided into dedicated subchannels assigned to individual VSPs and reusable subchannels shared among multiple VSPs, while RIS is employed to improve propagation conditions. We formulate a multi-VSP utility maximization problem that jointly optimizes subchannel assignment, transmit power, and RIS phase configuration while accounting for spectrum access costs, RIS leasing costs, and QoS constraints. The resulting mixed-integer non-linear program (MINLP) is intractable using conventional optimization methods. To address this challenge, the problem is modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP) and solved using deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Specifically, deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) and soft actor-critic (SAC) algorithms are developed and compared. Simulation results show that SAC outperforms DDPG in convergence speed, stability, and achievable utility, reaching up to 96% of the exhaustive search benchmark and demonstrating the potential of RIS to improve overall utility in multi-VSP scenarios.

AI.tldr: RIS-aided spectrum sharing framework for vertical service providers using DRL to optimize resource allocation and RIS configuration, achieving near-optimal utility.
AI.motivation: To address interference concerns with RIS while demonstrating that properly controlled RIS can enhance QoS in multi-VSP spectrum sharing scenarios within MNO ecosystems.
AI.method: Formulated MINLP problem for joint optimization of subchannel assignment, transmit power, and RIS phase configuration, then solved using DRL (DDPG and SAC algorithms) modeled as MDP.
AI.result: SAC outperforms DDPG in convergence speed, stability, and utility, achieving up to 96% of exhaustive search benchmark, demonstrating RIS's potential to improve overall utility.
AI.conclusion: Properly controlled RIS can effectively enhance QoS in multi-VSP spectrum sharing, with SAC-based DRL providing efficient solution for the complex joint optimization problem.

title: Four-Transistor Four-Diode (4T4D) Series/Parallel Chopper Module for Auto-Balancing STATCOM and Low Control and Development Complexity
summary: Static synchronous compensators (STATCOMs) manage reactive power compensation in modern power grids and have become essential for the integration of renewable energy sources such as wind farms. Cascaded H bridges have become the preferred topology for high-power STATCOMs, but balancing module capacitor voltages remains a persistent challenge. Conventional solutions equip every module with a voltage sensor -- a component that is costly, temperature-sensitive, and prone to aging-related failures. Recent parallel-capable module topologies can balance voltage through switched-capacitor operation. The latest developments reduced the sensor requirement from one per module to one per arm. However, these implementations require twice as many individual transistors compared to series-only topologies. We present a STATCOM solution based on the four-transistor four-diode (4T4D) series\,/\,parallel chopper cell. This topology achieves bidirectional parallelization with only four transistors per module -- exactly as many as a conventional full bridge. Furthermore, we propose a dual-loop control strategy that fully eliminates module voltage sensors by inferring voltage levels from the modulation index. This scheme also improves output quality by regulating the modulation depth. We validated our proposal through simulation and experiments. We built a prototype to interface the grid. The prototype further passed robustness tests with step change, current direction reversal, and grid disturbance. This work demonstrates the first modular STATCOM implementation that combines minimum transistor count with complete elimination of module voltage sensors.

AI.tldr: A novel STATCOM design using 4T4D series/parallel chopper cells achieves bidirectional parallelization with only 4 transistors per module (same as conventional full bridge) while completely eliminating module voltage sensors through dual-loop control that infers voltages from modulation index.
AI.motivation: STATCOMs are essential for renewable energy integration, but conventional cascaded H-bridge designs require costly, temperature-sensitive voltage sensors for each module. Recent parallel-capable topologies reduce sensors but double transistor count compared to series-only designs.
AI.method: Proposed STATCOM solution based on four-transistor four-diode (4T4D) series/parallel chopper cell topology with dual-loop control strategy that eliminates module voltage sensors by inferring voltage levels from modulation index while regulating modulation depth for improved output quality.
AI.result: Validated through simulation and experiments with a grid-interfacing prototype that passed robustness tests including step change, current direction reversal, and grid disturbance. Achieves bidirectional parallelization with only 4 transistors per module (same as conventional full bridge).
AI.conclusion: First modular STATCOM implementation combining minimum transistor count with complete elimination of module voltage sensors, addressing key challenges of cost, reliability, and complexity in high-power STATCOM systems for renewable energy integration.

title: Physics-informed structured learning of a class of recurrent neural networks with guaranteed properties
summary: This paper proposes a physics-informed learning framework for a class of recurrent neural networks tailored to large-scale and networked systems. The approach aims to learn control-oriented models that preserve the structural and stability properties of the plant. The learning algorithm is formulated as a convex optimisation problem, allowing the inclusion of linear matrix inequality constraints to enforce desired system features. Furthermore, when the plant exhibits structural modularity, the resulting optimisation problem can be parallelised, requiring communication only among neighbouring subsystems. Simulation results show the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: Physics-informed learning framework for recurrent neural networks in networked systems that preserves structural/stability properties through convex optimization with LMI constraints.
AI.motivation: Need for control-oriented models in large-scale networked systems that preserve plant structural and stability properties while enabling efficient learning.
AI.method: Physics-informed learning framework for recurrent neural networks formulated as convex optimization with linear matrix inequality constraints to enforce desired system features; leverages structural modularity for parallelization with neighbor-only communication.
AI.result: Simulation results demonstrate effectiveness of the proposed approach in learning control-oriented models that preserve system properties.
AI.conclusion: The physics-informed learning framework successfully enables learning of control-oriented models for networked systems while preserving structural/stability properties through convex optimization with LMI constraints, with potential for parallelization in modular systems.

title: Parameter-interval estimation for cooperative reactive sputtering processes
summary: Reactive sputtering is a plasma-based technique to deposit a thin film on a substrate. This contribution presents a novel parameter-interval estimation method for a well-established model that describes the uncertain and nonlinear reactive sputtering process behaviour. Building on a proposed monotonicity-based model classification, the method guarantees that all parameterizations within the parameter interval yield output trajectories and static characteristics consistent with the enclosure induced by the parameter interval. Correctness and practical applicability of the new method are demonstrated by an experimental validation, which also reveals inherent structural limitations of the well-established process model for state-estimation tasks.

AI.tldr: Novel parameter-interval estimation method for reactive sputtering process model with guaranteed consistency between parameterizations and output trajectories.
AI.motivation: Reactive sputtering is an uncertain and nonlinear plasma-based thin film deposition process requiring robust parameter estimation methods that account for model uncertainty.
AI.method: Monotonicity-based model classification approach that guarantees all parameterizations within estimated intervals yield output trajectories and static characteristics consistent with the parameter interval enclosure.
AI.result: Experimental validation demonstrates correctness and practical applicability of the method, while revealing inherent structural limitations of the established process model for state-estimation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed parameter-interval estimation method provides guaranteed consistency for reactive sputtering process modeling, though the established model shows structural limitations for state estimation.
